source_text: Ἐλέγομεν δὴ καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ὅτι αἱ μέν τινες εἰσὶ φωναὶ τοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως“ ὡς ἡ· „ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωὴ“ καὶ αἱ τούτοις παραπλήσιαι, αἱ δὲ τοῦ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν νοουμένου ἀνθρώπου ὡς ἡ τοῦ· „νῦν δέ με ζητεῖτε ἀποκτεῖναι, ἄνθρωπον, ὃς τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑμῖν λελάληκα. ἣν ἤκουσα παρὰ τοῦ πατρός.“ καὶ ἐνθάδε τοίνυν διαγράφει ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης σαρκὸς ἀσθενὲς καὶ τὸ τοῦ πνεύματος πρόθυμον. τὸ μὲν ἀσθενὲς ἐν τῷ „πάτερ, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι, παρελθέτω ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο.“ τὸ δὲ πρόθυμον τοῦ πνεύματος ἐν τῷ „πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς σύ.“ εἰ δὲ καὶ τὴν τάξιν τῶν λελεγμένων τηρῆσαι δεῖ. πρόσχες ὅτι πρότερον μὲν εἴρηται τὸ. ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, κατὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς ἓν τυγχάνον. ὕστερον δὲ τὰ κατὰ τὴν προθυμίαν τοῦ πνεύματος ὄντα πλείονα. ἓν μὲν γὰρ τὸ „πάτερ. εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι. παρελθέτω ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο,“ πλείονα δὲ τό τε „οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς σὺ“ καὶ τὸ „πάτερ μου, εἰ οὐ δύναται τοῦτο παρελθεῖν, ἐὰν μὴ αὐτὸ πίω, γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου.“ τηρητέον δὲ καὶ τὸ μὴ εἰρῆσθαι μέν· „ἀπελθέτω ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο,“ λελέχθαι δὲ εὐσεβῶς καὶ μεθ᾿ ὑποτιμήσεως ὅλον τοῦτο· „πάτερ, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι. παρελθέτω ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο.“ οἶδα δέ τινα καὶ τοιαύτην εἰς τὸν τόπον διήγησιν, ὅτι ὁρῶν ὁ σωτὴρ οἷα ὁ λαὸς καὶ Ἱερουσαλὴμ πείσεται ἐπὶ τῇ ἐκδικήσει τῶν κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ τετολμημένων ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων, οὐ δι᾿ ἄλλο τι ἢ διὰ τὸ πρὸς ἐκείνους φιλάνθρωπον θέλων μὴ παθεῖν τὸν λαὸν ἃ ἔμελλε πάσχειν φησὶ τὸ „πάτερ. εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι. παρελθέτω ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο“· ὡς εἰ ἔλεγεν· ἐπεὶ ἐκ τοῦ με πιεῖν τουτὶ τὸ τῆς κολάσεως ποτήριον ὅλον ἔθνος ὑπὸ σοῦ ἐγκαταλειφθήσεται, εὔχομαι. εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι, παρελθεῖν „ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο,“ ἵνα μὴ ἡ μερίς σου τολμήσασα κατ᾿ ἐμοῦ πάντῃ ὑπὸ σοῦ ἐγκαταλειφθῇ. ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ, ὥς φησιν ὁ Κέλσος. μήτ᾿ ἀλγεινόν τι μήτ᾿ ἀνιαρὸν τῷ Ἰησοῦ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦτον ἐγίνετο, πῶς ἂν οἱ μετὰ ταῦτα παραδείγματι τοῦ ὑπομένειν τὰ δι᾿ εὐσέβειαν ἐπίπονα ἐδύναντο χρήσασθαι Ἰησοῦ. μὴ παθόντι μὲν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα μόνον δὲ δόξαντι πεπονθέναι;
pass_a_gloss: We said indeed also in the things above that some utterances (φωναί) are of the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) 'of all creation (κτίσις)' in Jesus, such as 'I am the way (ὁδός) and the truth (ἀλήθεια) and the life (ζωή)' and those like these, but others of the man (ἄνθρωπος) understood (νοουμένου) according to him, such as 'But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth which I heard from the Father.' And here then he describes (διαγράφει) in his human [nature] (τὸ ἀνθρώπινον) both the weakness (τὸ ἀσθενές) of human flesh (σάρξ) and the willingness/eagerness (τὸ πρόθυμον) of the spirit (πνεῦμα): the weakness in 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me'; the willingness of the spirit in 'Yet not as I will, but as you.' And if one must also keep the order (τάξις) of the things said, attend that first is said what is, as one might say, according to the weakness of the flesh, being one; afterwards the things according to the willingness of the spirit, being more (πλείονα). For one is 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,' but more are both 'Not as I will, but as you' and 'My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.' One must observe also that it is not said 'Let this cup go away (ἀπελθέτω) from me,' but this whole is said piously (εὐσεβῶς) and with deference/modest qualification (μεθ᾿ ὑποτιμήσεως): 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.' I know also such an exposition (διήγησις) of the place: that the Saviour (σωτήρ), seeing what the people (λαός) and Jerusalem would suffer in the avenging (ἐκδίκησις) of the things dared (τετολμημένων) against him by Jews, for nothing else than for his love of humankind (τὸ φιλάνθρωπον) toward them, wishing the people not to suffer what it was about to suffer, says 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me'; as if he said: since from my drinking this cup of punishment (κόλασις) a whole nation (ἔθνος) will be forsaken (ἐγκαταλειφθήσεται) by you, I pray, if it is possible, that this cup pass from me, so that your portion (μερίς), having dared against me, may not be wholly forsaken by you. But also if, as Celsus says, neither anything painful nor grievous happened to Jesus at this time, how could those after these things use Jesus as an example (παράδειγμα) of enduring (ὑπομένειν) the toils (ἐπίπονα) for piety's sake (δι᾿ εὐσέβειαν), [he] not having suffered human things but only having seemed (δόξαντι) to have suffered?
pass_b_english: We said earlier too that some sayings belong to the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15) who was in Jesus, such as “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6) and others like it, while others belong to the man understood to be in him, such as “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from the Father” (John 8:40). So here too, in his human nature, he portrays both the weakness of human flesh and the willingness of the spirit (Matthew 26:41): the weakness in “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and the willingness of the spirit in “Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).

And if we must also keep to the order of what was said, notice that what belongs, so to speak, to the weakness of the flesh comes first and is a single saying, while what belongs to the willingness of the spirit comes afterward and runs to several. The single saying is “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); the several are both “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39) and “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42). We should also observe that he did not say, “Let this cup go away from me,” but that the whole was said reverently and with humble reserve: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

I know also an explanation of the passage along these lines. The Saviour saw what the people and Jerusalem would suffer in punishment for what the Jews had dared to do against him. For no other reason than his love for them, wishing the people not to suffer what they were about to suffer, he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” It is as if he were saying: Since, through my drinking this cup of punishment, a whole nation will be abandoned by you, I pray, if it is possible, that “this cup pass from me,” so that your portion, which has dared to act against me, may not be wholly abandoned by you.

Besides, if, as Celsus says, nothing painful or grievous befell Jesus at that time, how could those who came after him use Jesus as an example of enduring hardships for the sake of godliness, if he did not suffer what human beings suffer but only seemed to have suffered?

choices.term: τοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ πρωτοτόκου πάσης κτίσεως
choices.why: τοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ πρωτοτόκου πάσης κτίσεως: 'the firstborn "of all creation" in Jesus' -> 'the "firstborn of all creation" who was in Jesus' (quotation now covers the whole phrase of Colossians 1:15; relative clause makes the sense plain)
ἓν ... πλείονα: calque 'is a single thing ... is more ... the more are' -> 'a single saying ... runs to several ... the several are'

verified: Colossians 1:15; John 14:6; John 8:40 (Origen's 'from the Father' kept and noted); Matthew 26:39, 26:41, 26:42; 'as Celsus says' correctly reflects Celsus's 2.23 argument that a willing god would feel no pain

translator_notes: ‘We said earlier’ refers back to Origen’s earlier distinction between the sayings of the divine Word and of the man in Jesus (Book 2.9). John 8:40: Origen reads ‘from the Father’ (παρὰ τοῦ πατρός) where the usual Gospel text has ‘from God’; rendered as Origen quotes it. ‘Weakness of the flesh ... willingness of the spirit’ echoes Matthew 26:41 (τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής). ‘μεθ᾿ ὑποτιμήσεως’ (with a modest, deferential qualification) rendered ‘with humble reserve’; Origen’s point is the contrast between ἀπελθέτω (go away) and παρελθέτω (pass by) with ‘if it is possible’. ‘your portion’ (ἡ μερίς σου) for God’s people may echo Deuteronomy 32:9 (LXX ‘the Lord’s portion is his people’); possible allusion only, not cited inline. The clause ‘as Celsus says’ introduces a paraphrase of Celsus’s argument from 2.23, not his exact words, so no quotation marks. The quotations inside the ‘as if he were saying’ paraphrase keep the Gospel words in quotation marks as Origen marks them.
